rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its "Substack says its top creators earned $400M — the number it won't break down is the story" turns a disclosure gap into a reporter's question; B keeps "Substack's new video feed puts a newsletter platform in the ring with YouTube and TikTok," which is a competitor claim the fact block does not earn. A has one shaky no-ad-model assertion, but B repeatedly promotes its own proof gaps into headlines.
gaps_in_A: "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" asserts no-ad economics the update does not give; the proof section later admits it still needs confirmation.
"its revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions" overstates the business model. The update gives a 10% subscription cut, not proof that this is Substack's only revenue line.
"native video plus a TikTok-style feed completes a visible identity change" is a little too final. The facts support a media-app push, not a completed abandonment of newsletters.
gaps_in_B: "all-in-video media app" is invented heat. The update says native video and podcasts, not that Substack has gone all-in on video.
"puts a newsletter platform in the ring with YouTube and TikTok" is the bad kept angle. TikTok-style feed is supplied; YouTube/TikTok competitive threat is not.
"short-form, algorithmic-style feed" smuggles in mechanics the update does not state. TikTok-style does not automatically mean algorithmic ranking or short-form video.

"The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" reaches a conclusion the facts cannot carry. Creator earnings and paid subscriptions do not prove Substack's own financial health.
